post.title: How LinkedIn Made $19.8 Billion From Your Job Hunt (Without Charging Most of You)
post.ig: Most job seekers pay LinkedIn nothing, yet it made $19.8 billion in fiscal 2026. Here's who really pays.

post.yt_desc:
LinkedIn brought in $19.8 billion in Microsoft's fiscal 2026 (the year ending June 30, 2026), up 11%, even though most of its 1.3 billion-plus members never pay a cent. This video explains how Microsoft's $26.2 billion purchase from 2016 makes money from four lines: hiring tools for employers, Premium subscriptions, ads and Sales Navigator. We chart LinkedIn's revenue from fiscal 2018 to 2026, work out what it earns per member and what Premium Career costs per year, and look at the risks, from hiring slowdowns to the AI application flood and Microsoft's new reporting.

CHAPTERS

Fiscal 2026 is the last year Microsoft reported LinkedIn revenue as its own line; from fiscal 2027 it is split across other lines. Revenue totals are revenue, not profit, and use Microsoft's latest restated figures.

Sources: Microsoft Form 10-K annual reports, fiscal 2017 to fiscal 2026 (latest filed July 2026, via Microsoft Investor Relations); Microsoft 2026 Annual Report; Microsoft earnings materials, fiscal 2024 to 2026; Microsoft Form 8-K (Sept 2026) via Windows Report and Northeast Times; LinkedIn Form 8-K (June 13, 2016); LinkedIn fourth quarter and full year 2015 results (Feb 4, 2016); TechCrunch (Jan 15 and Jan 29, 2025); The New York Times via eWeek (June 2025); StaffingIndustry Analysts (2025); Premium Career prices via Lilach Bullock (Oct 2026) and Technobezz (Nov 2026).

News and education, not financial advice.
